title: How Decipherment Works
description: What the successful cases teach about scripts, languages and footholds

concepts.title: Script and Language Are Two Problems
concepts.contentHtml:
A writing system and the language it records are separate unknowns, and every decipherment story turns on which of the two was missing. The script is the set of signs and the rules for using them; the language is the speech those signs encode. Solve the script and you can pronounce a text. Only knowledge of the language lets you understand it.

The solved cases sort neatly. Linear B and the Maya glyphs were unknown scripts recording languages that could be recovered. Once Michael Ventris assigned sound values in 1952, Linear B turned out to be an early form of Greek, and Classic Maya inscriptions proved to be in a language close to the Ch'olan Mayan languages still spoken today. Hittite was the reverse. Its tablets used Babylonian cuneiform, so scholars could sound them out years before Bedřich Hrozný showed in 1915 what language they recorded.

Some scripts are only half solved. Etruscan is written in an alphabet borrowed from Greek and can be read aloud with confidence, but the language has no close living relative, so much of its vocabulary is uncertain. Meroitic, used in the kingdom of Kush in what is now Sudan, had the values of its 23 signs worked out by Francis Llewellyn Griffith between about 1909 and 1911, using royal names that also appear in Egyptian hieroglyphs. Its language is still poorly understood, though Claude Rilly has argued that it belongs to the Northern East Sudanic branch of Nilo-Saharan.

The hardest situation is an unknown script recording an unidentified language. Most of the scripts that still resist reading sit exactly there.

concepts.title: Footholds: Bilinguals, Names and Relatives
concepts.contentHtml:
No successful decipherment started from nothing. Across the solved cases three kinds of foothold recur, and the major breakthroughs nearly always combined at least two of them.

Bilinguals give the same content in a known and an unknown language. The Rosetta Stone (196 BCE) repeats one decree in Greek and in Egyptian; Darius I's inscription at Behistun tells one story in Old Persian, Elamite and Babylonian; the Phoenician and Luwian hieroglyphic texts at Karatepe in Turkey, found in the late 1940s, settled many readings of Luwian hieroglyphs. A bilingual is rarely complete. Much of the Rosetta Stone's hieroglyphic section is broken away, and nobody knew at first how its sections lined up.

Proper names of rulers, gods and places tend to keep roughly the same pronunciation across languages, so they leak sound values. Champollion used Ptolemy and Cleopatra, Georg Friedrich Grotefend used Darius and Xerxes, Ventris used Cretan place names such as Knossos and Amnisos, and Griffith used the names of Kushite rulers.

A known related language lets you recognize the words that sound values produce. Coptic did this for Egyptian; Hebrew, Aramaic and Arabic did it for Akkadian and Ugaritic; later Greek did it for Linear B. Where no relative exists, large bilingual resources must substitute. Sumerian, which has no known relatives, was read largely through Sumerian and Akkadian word lists compiled by Babylonian scribes themselves. The footholds compound: names give sounds, sounds give words, a relative language identifies them, and grammar checks the result.

concepts.title: Counting Signs
concepts.contentHtml:
Before reading anything, decipherers count. The number of distinct signs is the cheapest clue to how a script works, because each type of writing needs a characteristic number of signs.

  • An alphabet or consonant script needs roughly 20 to 40: Phoenician had 22, Greek 24, Ugaritic about 30.
  • A syllabary, with one sign per syllable such as ka, ke, ki, needs roughly 40 to 100: Japanese kana have 46 basic signs, Cherokee 85, Linear B about 87 syllabic signs plus a separate set of word signs.
  • A logo-syllabic script mixes word signs with sound signs and runs to hundreds: Egyptian hieroglyphs, Mesopotamian cuneiform and Maya glyphs.

Counts shaped real decipherments. In the 1770s Carsten Niebuhr counted 42 signs in the simplest of the three scripts at Persepolis and concluded that it was alphabetic; it is in fact a semi-syllabary of about 36 phonetic signs, close enough to point the way. When the tablets from Ras Shamra in Syria proved in 1929 to use fewer than 30 signs, Charles Virolleaud saw at once that this cuneiform-looking script had to be an alphabet. For Linear B, a count near 90 implied that each sign stood for a consonant plus a vowel, which is the logic behind Ventris's grid.

Counts need care. A small corpus undercounts, because rare signs may never turn up, and specialists disagree over whether two similar shapes are one sign or two. The Phaistos Disc shows 45 distinct signs, a syllabary-sized number, but its roughly 240 stamped signs are far too few to test any reading.

title: Egyptian Hieroglyphs
description: From symbolic fantasy to Champollion's phonetic system

concepts.title: Symbols Without Sounds: Horapollo and Kircher
concepts.contentHtml:
Egyptian hieroglyphs were in use for well over 3,000 years. The last dated hieroglyphic inscription is a graffito in the temple of Philae carved on 24 August 394 CE; the last dated Demotic text, at the same temple, comes from 452 CE. Soon afterward nobody could read either. Greek and Roman writers who described hieroglyphs mostly assumed that they were symbols of ideas rather than records of speech.

That assumption was codified in the Hieroglyphica, a Greek treatise attributed to Horapollo and usually dated to the fourth or fifth century CE. A manuscript found on the Greek island of Andros in the early fifteenth century reached Florence, and the text was printed in 1505. It explains signs as allegories. A vulture means "mother", it says, because all vultures are female. The meaning is right, since the vulture sign does write the Egyptian word for mother, but the reason is invented zoology. Renaissance scholars treated the book as a key to ancient wisdom.

The Jesuit polymath Athanasius Kircher (1602 to 1680) took this approach furthest. In Oedipus Aegyptiacus (1652 to 1654) he rendered short hieroglyphic texts as long mystical statements, and almost none of it was right. Yet Kircher also published on Coptic, the latest stage of the Egyptian language, and argued correctly that it descended from the language of the pharaohs. That idea became one of Champollion's tools.

The episode shows how a wrong theory of what kind of script you face can absorb unlimited effort. A symbolic reading can explain any sign and predicts nothing.

concepts.title: The Rosetta Stone and Thomas Young
concepts.contentHtml:
In July 1799, during Napoleon's invasion of Egypt, French soldiers rebuilding a fort near Rashid (Rosetta) in the Nile Delta found a broken slab of granodiorite. It carries a decree issued by a council of priests at Memphis in 196 BCE honoring the young king Ptolemy V. The text appears three times: in hieroglyphs, in Demotic (the cursive script of everyday Egyptian), and in Greek. That is two languages in three scripts. Under the Capitulation of Alexandria in 1801 the stone passed to the British, and it has been in the British Museum since 1802.

The Greek could be read at once, so the stone came with its own answer key. Using it was another matter. The top of the hieroglyphic section is lost, and nobody knew how the Egyptian words lined up with the Greek. In 1802 Antoine-Isaac Silvestre de Sacy and the Swedish diplomat Johan David Åkerblad located proper names in the Demotic and proposed sound values for some of its signs.

The British polymath Thomas Young (1773 to 1829) took up the stone around 1814. He confirmed that the oval rings called cartouches enclose royal names, identified Ptolemy's name, and assigned sound values to several signs in an anonymous 1819 article for the Encyclopaedia Britannica. By one later tally, about half of his values were right and the rest partly right or wrong. He also saw that Demotic and hieroglyphs were related.

Young's limit was his theory. He believed phonetic spelling was a special device for foreign names such as Ptolemy, and that native Egyptian words were written symbolically. That left most of the script out of reach.

concepts.title: Champollion, Coptic and the Cartouches
concepts.contentHtml:
Jean-François Champollion (1790 to 1832) had learned Coptic as a teenager. Coptic is written in Greek letters with vowels, so it let him test proposed sound values against real Egyptian words, something Young could not do.

Champollion compared two cartouches. Ptolemy was on the Rosetta Stone. A second name came from an obelisk at Philae, removed by William John Bankes to his estate at Kingston Lacy in England, whose base carries a Greek inscription naming Ptolemy and Cleopatra. If the second cartouche spelled Cleopatra, the two names should share signs for p, o and l in the expected positions, and they did. The t of Ptolemy and the t of Cleopatra were written with different signs, which showed that the script had homophones: different signs for the same sound.

In mid-September 1822, working from copies of temple reliefs, Champollion read native names. One cartouche held a sun disk (Coptic re, "sun"), a sign he linked to Coptic mise, "to give birth", and a sign for s: Ramesses. Phonetic signs were writing Egyptian words, not just foreign names. A family story has him running to his brother's office shouting "Je tiens l'affaire!" ("I've got it!") and collapsing. On 27 September 1822 he presented his Lettre à M. Dacier, addressed to the secretary of the Académie des Inscriptions in Paris, with Young in the audience.

The full system came in his Précis du système hiéroglyphique (1824): hieroglyphs mix signs for one, two or three consonants, signs for whole words, and silent determinatives that mark a word's category. Vowels were mostly not written; Coptic supplied them.

title: Cuneiform and Its Languages
description: From Persian royal names to Akkadian, Sumerian, Hittite and Ugaritic

concepts.title: Grotefend, Rawlinson and Behistun
concepts.contentHtml:
Cuneiform, wedge-shaped signs pressed into clay, was used in the Near East from about 3200 BCE into the first century CE. Unlike Egyptian, it was never tied to a single language. It was adapted for Sumerian, Akkadian, Elamite, Hittite and others, and the Persian kings had a simpler cuneiform-looking script devised for their own language, Old Persian.

Old Persian was the way in. Inscriptions at Persepolis, copied by Carsten Niebuhr, stood in three scripts side by side. In 1802 Georg Friedrich Grotefend, a schoolteacher in Göttingen, guessed that they were royal inscriptions following the formula of later Sasanian ones: "X, great king, king of kings, son of Y". In two texts he found a chain: king, son of a king, son of a man who was not a king. That fit Xerxes, son of Darius, son of Hystaspes, Darius's father, who never reigned. He got the names and a handful of sign values right, and his work won little recognition at the time.

Henry Creswicke Rawlinson, an officer of the British East India Company, did the decisive work at Behistun (Bisitun) in western Iran. There, around 520 BCE, Darius I had his account of how he seized power carved high on a cliff in Old Persian, Elamite and Babylonian. Rawlinson copied the inscription between 1835 and 1847 from ladders and ropes; in 1847 a local Kurdish boy he hired made paper squeezes of the hardest-to-reach Babylonian text. He published the Old Persian with a translation in 1846 and 1847.

Behistun did for cuneiform what the Rosetta Stone did for Egyptian: a long multilingual text in which the version that could be read opened the others.

concepts.title: Akkadian and the 1857 Test
concepts.contentHtml:
The Babylonian version was far harder. Akkadian cuneiform has several hundred signs, mixing word signs with syllables, and many signs have more than one sound value, a property called polyphony. In the 1840s and 1850s the Irish clergyman Edward Hincks showed that the signs were syllabic and that polyphony was real. Once the language was recognized as Semitic, Hebrew, Aramaic and Arabic supplied vocabulary and grammar to test readings against. Akkadian is now classed as East Semitic, with Assyrian and Babylonian as its main dialects.

Polyphony made skeptics doubt the whole enterprise: a script in which one sign could be read several ways looked like a license to invent. In 1857 the Royal Asiatic Society in London ran a test proposed by William Henry Fox Talbot. A newly found clay prism inscription of the Assyrian king Tiglath-Pileser I (reigned c. 1114 to 1076 BCE) was translated independently by Talbot, Rawlinson, Hincks and the German-born French scholar Jules Oppert, who submitted their versions under seal. A committee that included the historian George Grote and the Cambridge polymath William Whewell compared them and found broad agreement on the sense, with differences in detail.

The test did not prove every reading. It showed something harder to fake: four people working apart, on a text none of them had studied, reached the same meaning. Independent agreement on fresh material has been the standard for judging decipherments ever since.

concepts.title: Sumerian, Hittite and Ugaritic
concepts.contentHtml:
Reading Akkadian exposed other languages hidden in the same script. Some tablets held a language that was not Semitic at all, which scholars named Sumerian. From the 1870s Joseph Halévy argued that it was a secret code invented by Babylonian priests rather than a real language; large finds of texts written only in Sumerian, starting with French excavations at Telloh (ancient Girsu) in 1877, helped settle the question. Sumerian is a language isolate with no known relatives, so it was read through bilingual Sumerian and Akkadian texts and word lists made by scribes who kept it alive as a learned language long after it stopped being spoken.

Hittite was the classic readable script with an unknown language. Excavations led by Hugo Winckler at Boğazköy (ancient Hattusa) in central Anatolia from 1906 recovered thousands of tablets that could be sounded out but not understood. In 1915 the Czech scholar Bedřich Hrozný announced that Hittite was Indo-European. A famous sentence helped: nu NINDA-an ezzateni wātar-ma ekuteni, "now you will eat bread and drink water". NINDA is a Sumerian word sign for bread, ezza- recalls German essen and Latin edo, and wātar recalls English water. Hittite is the earliest well-documented Indo-European language.

Ugaritic shows how fast decipherment can go when the footholds line up. Tablets excavated at Ras Shamra in Syria from 1929 used about 30 signs, so the script had to be an alphabet. Assuming a Semitic language, Hans Bauer, Édouard Dhorme and Charles Virolleaud worked out the values independently within about a year, in 1930.

title: Linear B and the Maya Glyphs
description: Two twentieth-century breakthroughs that overturned expert expectations

concepts.title: Linear B: Kober, Ventris and a Greek Surprise
concepts.contentHtml:
Arthur Evans began excavating Knossos on Crete in 1900 and found thousands of clay tablets in a script he called Linear B. Evans held that the Minoans spoke a non-Greek language, and his authority shaped the field for decades. Carl Blegen found a second archive at Pylos on the Greek mainland in 1939, and Emmett L. Bennett Jr. published a standardized sign list in 1951.

Alice Kober (1906 to 1950), a classicist at Brooklyn College, refused to guess at sound values. In papers from 1945 to 1948 she showed, using sets of related words now called Kober's triplets, that Linear B words changed their endings, so the language was inflected. The way signs varied where stem met ending implied that some signs shared a consonant and others shared a vowel. She died in 1950.

Michael Ventris (1922 to 1956), an architect who had heard Evans lecture as a schoolboy in 1936, built on that logic. He arranged the signs in a grid: same row, same consonant; same column, same vowel, all before assigning any sounds. In 1952 he tried Cretan place names on words found mainly at Knossos, such as ko-no-so (Knossos), a-mi-ni-so (Amnisos) and tu-ri-so (Tylissos). The values held, and the words read as Greek. He had expected something like Etruscan and called his Greek trial "a frivolous digression" in a work note of June 1952. He announced the result on BBC radio on 1 July 1952.

The Cambridge philologist John Chadwick joined him, and they published the case jointly in 1953. A tablet from Pylos, read in 1953, became the classic check: beside drawings of three-legged cauldrons stood ti-ri-po-de, tripods, and beside cups with four handles, qe-to-ro-we, four-handled.

concepts.title: Landa's "Alphabet" and Knorozov
concepts.contentHtml:
Maya scribes wrote from at least the late centuries BCE until after the Spanish conquest, on stone monuments, painted pottery and bark-paper books. Spanish clergy destroyed most of the books. In 1562 the Franciscan friar Diego de Landa held an auto-da-fé at Maní in Yucatán at which Maya books were burned. Only four Maya codices survive.

Landa also wrote the main key. His Relación de las cosas de Yucatán, written around 1566 and known from an abridged copy that Charles Étienne Brasseur de Bourbourg found in Madrid and published in 1864, includes an "alphabet". Landa had asked Maya informants to write Spanish letters, and they wrote glyphs for the sounds of the letter names, so for "b", pronounced be, they drew the sign for the syllable be. Read as an alphabet, the list produced nonsense, which discredited phonetic approaches for decades. Meanwhile Ernst Förstemann, a librarian in Dresden, worked out the calendar and Venus tables of the Dresden Codex in the late nineteenth century, so the numbers were readable long before the words.

J. Eric S. Thompson, the most influential Mayanist of the mid-twentieth century, held that the glyphs were largely ideographic and concerned with time, astronomy and gods. In 1952 Yuri Knorozov, working in Leningrad, argued that Landa's list was a partial syllabary and that Maya writing combined word signs with syllable signs, like Egyptian or Japanese. A word such as kutz, "turkey", could be spelled ku-tzu, with the final vowel silent and usually echoing the one before it. Thompson rejected the idea, and Cold War suspicion of a Soviet scholar slowed its acceptance in the West until the 1970s and 1980s.

concepts.title: Proskouriakoff and the Palenque Round Tables
concepts.contentHtml:
Even phonetic readings would matter little if the inscriptions only recorded calendars and gods. In 1958 Heinrich Berlin identified "emblem glyphs" tied to particular cities. In 1960 Tatiana Proskouriakoff (1909 to 1985), a Russian-born architect and archaeologist at the Carnegie Institution of Washington, published a study of the monuments of Piedras Negras in Guatemala. The dated stelae fell into series, and no series spanned more than a human lifetime. Each began with a date marked by an "upended frog" glyph, followed some years later by a date marked by the so-called toothache glyph. She argued that these were births and accessions of rulers, and that each series covered a reign. The inscriptions recorded dynastic history: named kings and queens, their births, wars and deaths.

Knorozov's phonetics and Proskouriakoff's history came together in the 1970s. At the first Mesa Redonda de Palenque, held at Palenque in Chiapas, Mexico, in December 1973 and organized by Merle Greene Robertson, Linda Schele, Peter Mathews and Floyd Lounsbury worked out much of the city's royal sequence, including the king now called K'inich Janaab Pakal, who reigned from 615 to 683 CE. The round tables continued as working meetings where readings were proposed and tested.

Since then, syllabic readings have multiplied, and most Classic Maya inscriptions can now be read in large part, though some signs remain unread or disputed. Maya history now has a political narrative of rival kingdoms, such as Tikal and Calakmul, that the glyphs themselves supply.

title: Ciphers Broken by Historians and Codebreakers
description: Deliberately hidden texts, from Louis XIV's codebook to Mary Stuart's letters

concepts.title: Codes, Ciphers and the Great Cipher
concepts.contentHtml:
A cipher differs from a lost script: it hides a known language on purpose, and its makers want it to resist. The tools overlap all the same. Codebreakers count symbols, look for repeats, and guess a probable word, called a crib, much as decipherers use proper names. A code replaces whole words or phrases with groups from a codebook; a cipher replaces letters or syllables by rule. Early modern diplomats used nomenclators that mixed both.

Antoine Rossignol and his son Bonaventure served as cryptographers to Louis XIV in the seventeenth century, and their Great Cipher protected sensitive royal correspondence. Long after the Rossignols died, letters written in it sat in French archives unread.

In the 1890s the French army cryptographer Étienne Bazeries spent about three years on it, finishing around 1893. The texts used 587 different numbers: too many for letters, too few for a full codebook of words. Bazeries guessed that they stood for syllables, the same reasoning that sign counts give for scripts. He took a repeated sequence, 124-22-125-46-345, to be les-en-ne-mi-s, "les ennemis" ("the enemies"), and built outward. The system also contained traps: nulls, numbers that meant nothing, and a group that told the reader to delete the one before it.

One decrypted letter to Marshal Nicolas de Catinat ordered the arrest of General Vivien de Bulonde, who had abandoned a siege in Piedmont in 1691. Bazeries suggested that Bulonde was the Man in the Iron Mask, but the two number groups he read as "mask" and a full stop occur only once, and historians do not accept the identification.

concepts.title: The Zimmermann Telegram
concepts.contentHtml:
In January 1917 the German foreign secretary, Arthur Zimmermann, sent an encoded telegram for the German minister in Mexico, Heinrich von Eckardt. Germany was about to resume unrestricted submarine warfare. If the United States entered the war, Mexico was to be offered an alliance and help to recover lost territory in Texas, New Mexico and Arizona.

British naval intelligence intercepted it. In the codebreaking office known as Room 40, Nigel de Grey and William Montgomery produced a partial decrypt within days. The message was in German diplomatic code 0075, a codebook of about 10,000 groups that Room 40 had only partly reconstructed. Its chief, Admiral William Reginald Hall, faced a problem: publishing the text would reveal that Britain was reading diplomatic cable traffic, including messages carried on American lines. The German embassy in Washington had forwarded the message to Mexico by commercial telegraph in an older code, 13040, which Room 40 could read far better. A British agent obtained the Mexico City copy, giving both a cleaner text and a cover story: the leak could plausibly have happened in Mexico.

Britain gave the text to the American ambassador, Walter Hines Page, in late February. It appeared in American newspapers on 1 March 1917, and Zimmermann publicly admitted that it was genuine a few days later. The United States declared war on Germany on 6 April 1917. Most historians see the submarine campaign as the main cause, with the telegram hardening opinion, especially in the West and Southwest.

For historians the episode is also a lesson in sources: how the text was obtained was kept secret for years, so the public account of 1917 was partly a cover story.

concepts.title: Copiale and Mary Stuart: Computers in the Archive
concepts.contentHtml:
The Copiale cipher is a 105-page eighteenth-century manuscript of about 75,000 handwritten characters, a mix of abstract symbols and Roman and Greek letters, that surfaced in the archive of the East Berlin Academy after the Cold War. In 2011 Kevin Knight of the University of Southern California, with Beáta Megyesi and Christiane Schaefer of Uppsala University, cracked it with computer help. Treating the Roman letters as the message failed. The unaccented Roman letters turned out to mark spaces between words, while the abstract symbols carried German in a homophonic substitution, with several symbols for common letters and a few for whole words. The text describes the rituals of a secret society in Wolfenbüttel, the Oculists, whose initiate was asked to read a blank page, given eyeglasses, and had a single eyebrow hair plucked.

George Lasry, Norbert Biermann and Satoshi Tomokiyo, searching the digitized collections of the Bibliothèque nationale de France for enciphered documents, found letters cataloged as Italian from the early sixteenth century. A computer search gave a partial key and the rest was done by hand. The language was French. Feminine grammatical forms, mentions of "my son", and the name of Francis Walsingham, Elizabeth I's spymaster, pointed to Mary, Queen of Scots. The team published in 2023: 57 letters from 1578 to 1584, mostly to the French ambassador Michel de Castelnau, in a cipher of 191 symbols. A few had been known from copies in English archives; most had not.

In both cases computers searched through possible keys while people supplied language, context and judgment.

title: New Tools and the Burden of Proof
description: Linear Elamite, machine learning, and what a decipherment must show

concepts.title: Linear Elamite: A Claimed Decipherment
concepts.contentHtml:
Elamite, the language of ancient Elam in southwestern Iran, is an isolate known mainly from cuneiform texts. Linear Elamite is a different script used roughly 2300 to 1850 BCE and known from only a few dozen inscriptions on stone, clay and silver vessels. A few names had been identified since the early twentieth century, thanks to the "Table au Lion" in the Louvre, a bilingual with Akkadian from the reign of King Puzur-Inshushinak.

In 2022 François Desset and colleagues (Kambiz Tabibzadeh, Matthieu Kervran, Gian Pietro Basello and Gianni Marchesi) published "The Decipherment of Linear Elamite Writing" in the Zeitschrift für Assyriologie. Their anchors were inscribed silver beakers carrying the names of rulers such as Shilhaha and Ebarat, kings already known from cuneiform sources. Matching names to sign sequences yielded sound values, which they extended across the corpus. They claim the script is almost entirely phonetic, a semi-syllabary of about 70 core signs, which would make it one of the oldest largely sound-based scripts known.

Reception is mixed, so this is best described as a claim with substantial support. Several leading specialists in Elamite and Mesopotamian studies have welcomed it. Others have raised objections. Michael Mäder has argued that a significant share of the signs are word signs, not purely phonetic. Some want fuller, checkable translations of the longer texts. Several key beakers belong to a private collection and lack a documented excavation context, which raises questions of authenticity and ethics; Desset himself has said he first assumed they were probably forgeries, until he examined them.

What would settle the matter is the test that settled Linear B: newly excavated texts that other scholars can read with the published values.

concepts.title: Machines as Decipherers
concepts.contentHtml:
Computational decipherment is tested on scripts that are already solved, because only then can success be measured. In 2010 Benjamin Snyder, Regina Barzilay and Kevin Knight gave a statistical model Ugaritic texts and separate Hebrew texts, with no translations between them. It matched 29 of the 30 Ugaritic letters to the right Hebrew letters and found the correct Hebrew cognate for about 60 percent of Ugaritic words that have one.

In 2019 Jiaming Luo and Barzilay of MIT, with Yuan Cao of Google, improved on the Ugaritic result with a neural model and tried Linear B against Greek, correctly matching 67.3 percent of cognates. A 2021 follow-up by Luo and colleagues tackled texts without word divisions and with no assumed relative. Their measure picked out the right related languages for Gothic and Ugaritic, and for Iberian it found no strong evidence of a link to Basque, in line with the majority scholarly view.

The limits are built in. These methods match an unknown script to a known related language and look for cognates, so they need both a plausible relative and enough text. An isolate known from a few dozen short inscriptions offers almost nothing to match. A different kind of tool restores damaged texts in scripts that can already be read. DeepMind's Ithaca, published in 2022, fills gaps in Greek inscriptions; in tests, historians alone restored 25 percent of the missing text correctly, and historians working with Ithaca reached 72 percent.

So far computing has helped most with ciphers, as with Copiale and Mary Stuart's letters, and with the slow work of building digital corpora, sign lists and statistics.

concepts.title: What a Decipherment Has to Prove
concepts.contentHtml:
Claimed decipherments are common and accepted ones are rare. The accepted cases share features that serve as a checklist.

  • Consistency: one set of sign values works across the whole corpus, not just on chosen passages.
  • Economy: each sign keeps a small, fixed set of values. A system that lets a sign mean whatever a passage needs can "read" anything.
  • A real language: the output has consistent grammar, and its words fit the context, such as numbers, drawings and where an object was found.
  • Prediction: the system reads texts found after it was fixed. The Pylos tripod tablet, read in 1953, matched Ventris's values with drawings made by a scribe who knew nothing of his grid.
  • Independent replication: other scholars using the published values get the same readings, as in the Royal Asiatic Society's sealed translations of 1857.

Failed claims usually break one of these rules: values adjusted text by text, a handful of favorable examples, or translations loose enough to fit any language. Corpus size matters as well. The Phaistos Disc, a single clay disk from Crete with about 240 stamped signs, has attracted many mutually incompatible "decipherments" because it is too short for any of them to be tested. Linear A, the Indus script, Rongorongo of Rapa Nui and Proto-Elamite remain open, mainly because they lack some combination of bilinguals, large corpora and an identified language.

A decipherment is settled by evidence that accumulates, and Linear Elamite is now going through exactly that filter.
